title: UMD students partner with NASA to create asteroid-observing spacecraft
excerpt: University of Maryland students are working with NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center to create a spacecraft that will help the agency study Apophis, an asteroid discovered in 2004.
content:
‘1-in-7,500-year opportunity’: UMD partners with NASA to create asteroid-observing spacecraft

11/26/2026 5:30 a.m. EST

What started as a class project for a graduate capstone course at the University of Maryland is becoming an earth-shattering space mission.

Some 90 students from the university have partnered with NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center to create a spacecraft that will help the agency study Apophis, an asteroid discovered in 2004.

“This is a one-in-7,500-year opportunity to have something that big come to us at Earth for us to study,” said Elena Wu, the UMD team’s project manager.

At first, researchers were concerned Apophis could hit Earth, Wu said, but they established that the planet is safe from the asteroid. It’s going to come very close, however.

Apophis won’t pass Earth until April 13, 2029, but the goal is to study the asteroid before its arrival and launch nearly a year earlier in June 2028. Earth’s gravity field is expected to alter Apophis’ appearance and trajectory when it passes. According to Wu, Apophis will come closer to Earth than some of the human-made satellites already here.

The mission, dubbed Terp Raptor, will precede other Apophis missions being conducted by NASA and the European Space Agency.

With the asteroid closing in, students and engineers have been laser focused on building the spacecraft. The small probe is made up of cubes roughly the size of a toaster.

That spacecraft will do two things: capture images of the asteroid as it flies by and measure it.

Collecting these photos will allow scientists to build a 3D model of the asteroid that will help them learn more about its composition, topology and history, said Max Weinstock, chief engineer on the Terp Raptor team.

The original team, a group of seven graduate students and a professor, started the project in 2024. NASA mentors came in to review the satellite, only to realize its potential for a mission.

Although the university has collaborated with NASA in the past, the TERP Raptor project marks the first time UMD students and staff have access to a dedicated lab space at the center in Greenbelt.

“UMD has never put a spacecraft up there in space before,” Wu said. “I’m just super proud of everyone and super proud of what we have going on.”

The original satellite was much larger and using it in a mission would have cost about $10 million, Wu said. Those costs fell significantly as the spacecraft’s design became smaller and more efficient and the team secured a ride for the satellite into space on a commercial rocket.

The total projected mission cost is about $1.5 million. Roughly $1.3 million of that is budgeted for hardware. The Terp Raptor team has locked down $640,000 from various partners, including NASA, George Mason University and the Aerospace Corp. UMD is crowdfunding the remaining balance.

The team began a preliminary design review last week. It hopes to have a final design by the spring so it can start building and testing the satellite by fall 2027. The goal is to get everything to the commercial flight host by February 2028.

The spacecraft will remain in orbit for months while engineers extract images and data. It eventually will float into deep space. Weinstock anticipates the mission will end within the first months of 2029.

The asteroid will be visible over parts of Europe, Northern Africa and Southern Asia.

“It would look like a small star passing through the sky but still close enough that it’s as if the light of the sun would reflect off of it,” Weinstock said. “You would absolutely be able to see it passing over us.”

Shayla Colon is an express reporter for The Banner. Before coming to Baltimore, she covered violence prevention and New York City for The New York Times and private markets for the Financial Times. She also reported on local government and communities in Connecticut and upstate New York for Hearst newspapers.
